title: Businesses, Competition and Profit
bigQuestion: What does it take for a business to earn a profit, and why does competition help buyers?

story.title: The School Store's First Month
story.kicker: The eighth graders opened a school store and found out that selling is the easy part.
paragraphs: In September, Ms. Ortiz's eighth-grade class opened a school store in an old supply closet. They sold pencils, snacks, water and hoodies with the school mascot on them. The principal agreed to lend them the room for $50 a month in rent (an example amount). The class voted on prices and made a big sign.

The first week felt like a win. Students lined up at lunch. The cash box filled with bills and coins. By the end of the month, the store had taken in $900 (an example amount). Some students wanted a pizza party right away. "We're rich!" said Devin.

Then Priya, the class treasurer, spread the receipts on a desk. The snacks had cost $300. The hoodies had cost $450. Rent was $50. Printing the sign had cost $25. And 12 hoodies were still sitting in a box, unsold, in sizes nobody wanted.

Priya did the math out loud. "We brought in $900. We spent $825. We kept $75." The room got quiet. Then someone asked the hard questions. Should they raise prices? Order fewer hoodies? What if the eighth graders down the hall opened their own store? This chapter follows those questions.
story.think: Did the store really make money in its first month? What would you change for month two?

lessons.title: Revenue and Costs
lessons.mainIdea: Revenue is the money a business takes in; costs are the money it spends to run.
reading: Start with the school store's cash box. Every sale adds money. Say the store sells 150 bags of chips at $1 each and 40 bottles of water at $1.50 each (example prices). Chips bring in 150 times $1, or $150. Water brings in 40 times $1.50, or $60. Together that is $210.

The money a business takes in from sales is its *revenue*. To find it, multiply the price by the number sold, then add up every product. Revenue is NOT the same as the money the business gets to keep. That is a common mistake, and it was Devin's mistake in the story.

A business also pays *costs*. Costs are the money spent to make and sell its goods. The store pays for the chips it buys to resell, the rent for the room and the paint for the sign. Some costs stay the same no matter how much you sell, like rent. These are *fixed costs*. Others grow with each sale, like the chips themselves. These are variable costs.

words.d: the total money a business takes in from sales; price times quantity sold
the money a business spends to make and sell its goods or services
costs that stay the same no matter how much a business sells, like rent

look.title: School Store Sales, One Week (example)
look.cite: Made-up example sales for a middle school store
look.prompt: What was the store's total revenue this week? Which product brought in the most?

check.q: A car wash washes 40 cars at $8 each (example price). What is its revenue?
check.why: Revenue is price times quantity: 40 times $8 equals $320.

check.q: Which of these is a fixed cost for a food truck?
choices: The ground beef for each taco
The napkins given with each order
check.why: The permit costs the same whether the truck sells 10 tacos or 1,000. The others rise with each sale.

check.q: Devin sees $900 in the cash box and says the store is rich. What mistake is he making?
choices: He is confusing revenue with profit
He is confusing supply with demand
He forgot the price of hoodies
check.why: $900 is revenue. The store must still subtract its costs to find what it keeps.

lessons.title: Profit and Loss
lessons.mainIdea: Profit is revenue minus costs; if costs are bigger than revenue, the business has a loss.
reading: Now use Priya's receipts. The store brought in $900. Its costs were $300 for snacks, $450 for hoodies, $50 for rent and $25 for the sign. Add the costs: 300 plus 450 plus 50 plus 25 equals $825. Then subtract: $900 minus $825 equals $75.

That $75 is the store's *profit*. Profit is what is left after a business pays all its costs. The rule is short: profit equals revenue minus costs. If the costs had been $950, the store would have a *loss* of $50. A loss means the business spent more than it took in.

Profit sends a signal. A big profit tells other sellers that people want this product, so more may enter the market. A loss tells a business to change something: cut costs, change prices or sell something else. Profit is also the reward owners get for taking a risk with their money and time.

words.d: the money left after a business pays all its costs; revenue minus costs
what happens when a business's costs are greater than its revenue

look.title: Month Two Choices
look.text: For month two, the school store has two ideas. Plan A: stop selling hoodies, which cost $450 and brought in only $360 (example amounts). Plan B: keep hoodies but order only the sizes that sold.
look.prompt: Did the hoodies earn a profit or a loss in month one? Which plan would you pick, and what do you give up?

check.q: A lemonade stand takes in $120 and spends $45 on lemons, sugar and cups (example amounts). What is its profit?
check.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $120 minus $45 equals $75.

check.q: A bakery has revenue of $2,000 and costs of $2,300 in one month (example amounts). What happened?
check.why: Costs are bigger than revenue. $2,300 minus $2,000 equals a $300 loss.

check.q: Many new shops open after one ice cream shop earns big profits. Why?
choices: Ice cream got cheaper to make
The profit signaled that people want ice cream
The first shop asked for help
check.why: High profits signal strong demand, which draws new sellers into the market.

lessons.title: Pricing for Profit
lessons.mainIdea: A higher price does not always mean more revenue, because buyers purchase fewer units.
reading: Should the store just raise prices? Try it with example numbers. At $1 a bag, the store sells 150 bags of chips, so revenue is $150. At $2 a bag, students buy only 60 bags, so revenue is 60 times $2, or $120. The higher price brought in LESS money. Many students bought cookies or brought chips from home.

Remember the law of demand. When the price goes up, the quantity demanded goes down. A business must think about both parts of revenue: price and quantity. Raising the price helps only if sales do not fall too much.

How much buyers react depends on the good. If there are many substitutes, buyers switch fast. If there are few substitutes, like water on a hot field day, buyers react less. Businesses test prices, watch what sells and adjust. That is why stores run sales and try new prices.

words.d: the amount of money a buyer pays for one unit of a good or service
a good that can be used in place of another, like cookies in place of chips

look.title: Chip Price Test (example)
look.cite: Made-up example price test for a school store
look.prompt: Find the revenue at each price (price times bags). Which prices bring in the most revenue?

check.q: Using the chip table, what is the revenue at $1.50 a bag?
check.why: 100 bags times $1.50 equals $150.

check.q: Using the chip table, which price brings in the LEAST revenue?
check.why: $0.50 times 200 is $100; $1.00 gives $150; $1.50 gives $150; $2.00 gives $120. $100 is the least.

check.q: Why can raising a price lower a store's revenue?
choices: Buyers purchase fewer units at the higher price
check.why: Revenue is price times quantity. If quantity falls enough, revenue drops even at a higher price.

lessons.title: One Owner or Partners
lessons.mainIdea: A sole proprietorship has one owner; a partnership has two or more who share the business.
reading: Think of a neighbor who runs a lawn-mowing business alone. She owns it all. She makes every choice and keeps every dollar of profit. This is a *sole proprietorship*, a business owned by one person. It is the most common kind of business in the United States, and it is easy to start.

But there is a big risk. If the business owes money it cannot pay, the owner may have to pay it from her own savings. This is called unlimited liability. Liability means legal responsibility for debts. Her car or savings could be at risk if the business fails.

Now picture two friends who open a bike repair shop. They each put in money and share the work and the profit. This is a *partnership*, a business owned by two or more people. Partners can pool money and skills. But they must agree on choices, and in a general partnership each partner can be responsible for the business's debts.

words.d: a business owned and run by one person, who keeps the profits and is responsible for the debts
a business owned by two or more people who share the work, profits and debts
legal responsibility for a business's debts

look.title: Going It Alone?
look.text: Jaden bakes great cakes and wants to sell them. His cousin Rosa is good with numbers and has $2,000 saved (an example amount). She offers to be his partner and split the profit half and half.
look.prompt: What would Jaden gain from a partnership? What would he give up? Would you take the deal?

check.q: A dog-walker runs her business alone and keeps all the profit. What kind of business is it?
check.why: A business owned by one person is a sole proprietorship.

check.q: What is one big risk of a sole proprietorship?
choices: The owner may have to pay business debts from personal savings
check.why: Sole proprietors have unlimited liability, so personal money can be used to pay business debts.

check.q: Why might two people form a partnership?
choices: To combine their money and skills
To keep all the profit for one person
check.why: Partners pool money, skills and work. They still share risk and profit.

lessons.title: Corporations
lessons.mainIdea: A corporation is a business that is its own legal unit, owned by shareholders who risk only what they invested.
reading: Big companies that make phones, cars or cereal are usually corporations. A *corporation* is a business that the law treats as separate from its owners. It can own property, sign contracts and borrow money in its own name.

The owners of a corporation are its *shareholders*. They own small pieces of the company called shares, or stock. Say a company has 1,000 shares and you buy 10 (an example). You own 10 divided by 1,000, or 1% of the company. If it earns a profit, it may pay part of it to shareholders.

The big advantage is limited liability. If the corporation fails, shareholders can lose the money they put in, but not their homes or savings. Selling shares also raises large amounts of money. The trade-offs: corporations cost more to set up, must follow more rules and file more reports, and owners may have little say in daily choices.

words.d: a business the law treats as separate from its owners, able to own property and borrow in its own name
a person who owns shares, or stock, in a corporation
owners can lose only the money they invested, not their personal property

look.title: Which Type Fits? (example counts)
look.cite: Made-up example: 10 businesses on one neighborhood street
look.prompt: What percent of the businesses on this example street are sole proprietorships? Why might small shops choose that type?

check.q: A company has 2,000 shares. You own 20 (example numbers). What percent of the company do you own?
check.why: 20 divided by 2,000 equals 0.01, which is 1%.

check.q: What is the main advantage of limited liability for shareholders?
choices: They can lose only the money they invested
check.why: Limited liability protects shareholders' personal property if the business fails.

check.q: Which is a trade-off of forming a corporation?
choices: The owner is personally responsible for all debts
It costs more to set up and has more rules
It can have only one owner
check.why: Corporations gain limited liability and easier fundraising, but they face higher setup costs and more rules.

lessons.title: Why More Sellers Help Buyers
lessons.mainIdea: Competition among many sellers usually pushes prices down and quality up.
reading: Back to the story. The eighth graders down the hall open a second store. Right away, things change. The first store sold water for $1.50 (an example price). The new store sells it for $1.25. Students walk down the hall to save a quarter. Soon the first store cuts its price to $1.25 too.

This is *competition*: sellers trying to win the same buyers. When buyers can choose, each seller has a reason to offer lower prices, better products or faster service. A store that charges too much or treats customers poorly loses sales to its rival.

Competition also pushes new ideas. The first store starts selling fruit cups, which the other store does not have. Competition is not always comfortable for sellers. Some lose money and close. But for buyers, more sellers usually mean lower prices and more choices.

words.d: the struggle among sellers to attract buyers by offering better prices, products or service
another business that tries to sell to the same buyers

look.title: Adam Smith on Self-Interest
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, Book I, Chapter 2
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. In your own words, why does the baker sell you bread? How does competition turn a seller's self-interest into good deals for buyers?

check.q: A town has one pizza shop. Three more open nearby. What will most likely happen to pizza prices?
choices: They will stay the same forever
check.why: More sellers compete for the same buyers, which usually pushes prices down.

check.q: Which is a way businesses compete besides price?
choices: Charging more for the same thing
Offering better quality or new products
check.why: Sellers can win buyers with quality, new products or better service, not only lower prices.

check.q: What did Adam Smith mean about the butcher and baker?
choices: They sell to us because it serves their own interest
They give food away for free
check.why: Smith argued that sellers serve buyers because it helps themselves, and trade benefits both sides.

lessons.title: When There Is Only One Seller
lessons.mainIdea: A monopoly is a market with only one seller, which can charge more and has less reason to improve.
reading: Now imagine the school allows only ONE store. There is no other place to buy water at lunch. The store raises water from $1.25 to $2 (example prices). Some students skip water, but many still buy it. They have no other choice nearby.

A market with only one seller of a good that has no close substitutes is a *monopoly*. A monopoly can often charge higher prices and sell less than a competitive market would. With no rival, it also has less reason to improve quality or service.

Some monopolies happen for good reasons. A company may hold a *patent*, a right from the government to be the only seller of a new invention for a set time. That reward encourages people to invent. A town often has one water system, because building two sets of pipes would waste money. Governments often set rules on the prices such services can charge.

words.d: a market with only one seller of a good that has no close substitutes
a government grant that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a set time

look.title: The Only Gas Station
look.text: A small town far from any highway has one gas station. The nearest other station is 40 miles away. The owner charges 50 cents a gallon more than stations in the city (an example).
look.prompt: Why can this owner charge more? What might happen if a second station opened in town?

check.q: Which is the best example of a monopoly?
choices: Ten coffee shops on one street
Three phone brands in a store
The only company allowed to sell water service in a town
check.why: A monopoly has only one seller with no close substitutes, like a single town water service.

check.q: Compared with a competitive market, a monopoly usually has:
choices: higher prices and less reason to improve
check.why: With no rivals, a monopoly can charge more and faces less pressure to improve.

check.q: Why does the government give patents, which create short-term monopolies?
choices: To help buyers pay less right away
check.why: A patent lets an inventor be the only seller for a set time, which rewards the work of inventing.

lessons.title: Keeping Markets Fair
lessons.mainIdea: Governments use antitrust laws to stop businesses from blocking competition.
reading: Sometimes businesses try to escape competition on purpose. Say the two school stores secretly agree to both charge $2 for water instead of $1.25 (example prices). Neither one loses customers, and students pay more. An agreement like this among rivals to fix prices hurts buyers.

Adam Smith warned about this back in 1776. The United States passed the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890. *Antitrust laws* are laws that ban price-fixing and other ways of blocking competition. The government can also study a merger. A *merger* is when two companies join into one. If it would leave buyers with too few choices, the government can try to stop it in court.

Economists debate how much to step in. Some say big firms can be efficient and lower costs, so the government should act only when buyers are clearly harmed. Others say giant firms can crush new rivals and should be watched more closely. Both sides agree that price-fixing among rivals hurts buyers.

words.d: laws that ban price-fixing and other actions that block competition
when two companies join together to form one company
a secret agreement among rival sellers to charge the same high price

look.title: Adam Smith's Warning
look.text: People of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment and diversion, but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776, Book I, Chapter 10
look.prompt: A conspiracy is a secret plan; a contrivance is a trick. What was Smith worried sellers might do when they meet? Which law today tries to stop it?

check.q: Two rival airlines secretly agree to raise fares on the same day. What is this called?
check.why: Rivals agreeing on prices is price-fixing, which antitrust laws ban.

check.q: In what year did the United States pass the Sherman Antitrust Act?
check.why: The Sherman Antitrust Act became law in 1890.

check.q: Why might the government try to block a merger of the two biggest companies in a market?
choices: Buyers could be left with too few choices
check.why: Antitrust officials act when a merger would cut competition and hurt buyers.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurs Take the Risk
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur starts a business, takes on risk and earns profit as the reward if it works.
reading: Every business starts with someone willing to try. An *entrepreneur* is a person who starts a business and takes on the risk. Say a teen named Leo spends $200 of his savings on a used snow blower (an example). If it snows a lot, he earns $600 clearing driveways. If it barely snows, he might earn only $100 and lose money.

That chance of losing is *risk*. The possible profit is the reward. Leo's profit in the snowy winter would be $600 minus $200, or $400. In the dry winter, $100 minus $200 is a loss of $100. Entrepreneurs start businesses because they believe the reward is worth the risk.

Starting a business also has an opportunity cost. Leo could have kept his $200 or spent his time on something else. Many new businesses fail. But entrepreneurs who succeed bring new products and jobs. They spot a need, like shoveled driveways on a busy street, and fill it.

words.d: a person who starts a new business and takes on the risk of losing money
the chance of losing money or something of value
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: The Phone Case Idea
look.text: Aisha wants to design and sell phone cases online. She needs $300 for supplies (an example). She could instead use that $300 for a summer camp she really wants.
look.prompt: What is Aisha's risk? What is her opportunity cost? What would help her decide?

check.q: Leo spends $200 on a snow blower and earns $600. What is his profit?
check.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $600 minus $200 equals $400.

check.q: What is the reward an entrepreneur hopes for in exchange for risk?
check.why: Profit is the reward for taking on the risk of starting a business.

check.q: Aisha spends her $300 on phone case supplies instead of camp. What is her opportunity cost?
choices: The summer camp she gave up
check.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best choice given up, which is the camp.

lessons.title: A Plan for the School Store
lessons.mainIdea: A business plan lists what you will sell, to whom, at what price, and how you expect to earn a profit.
reading: Before month two, Ms. Ortiz's class writes a *business plan*. A business plan is a written guide to how a business will work and make money. Theirs answers five questions. What will we sell? Who will buy it? What will we charge? What will it cost? How much profit do we expect?

The class uses its month-one numbers. They expect to sell 300 snacks at $1.25 each, or $375 (example numbers). The snacks cost $0.60 each, so 300 cost $180. Rent stays $50. Expected profit on snacks: $375 minus $180 minus $50 equals $145. They decide to order hoodies only after taking pre-orders, so none are left over.

A plan also names the competition, in this case the other store, and how to stand out. The class plans to sell fruit cups and open five minutes earlier. A plan does not guarantee success. But it makes owners check their numbers before they spend real money.

words.d: a written guide that explains what a business will sell, to whom, at what price, and how it expects to earn a profit
the total money a business takes in from sales; price times quantity sold

look.title: Month Two Plan (example)
look.cite: Made-up example business plan for a school store
look.prompt: Check the math: does revenue minus both costs equal the expected profit? What would profit be if rent rose to $80?

check.q: In the example plan, what would the expected profit be if rent rose from $50 to $80?
check.why: $375 minus $180 minus $80 equals $115.

check.q: Why did the class decide to take pre-orders for hoodies?
choices: To avoid leftover hoodies, a surplus
check.why: Pre-orders match the number made to the number wanted, so the store avoids unsold stock.

check.q: Which question does a business plan NOT need to answer?
choices: What is every student's favorite color?
check.why: A plan covers what to sell, to whom, the price, the costs and expected profit, not unrelated facts.

lessons.title: Workers, Wages and Unions
lessons.mainIdea: Wages are set mostly by the supply of and demand for workers; unions let workers bargain as a group.
reading: The school store needs cashiers. Workers are part of a market too. A *wage* is the payment a worker earns for work, often counted per hour. Say a shop pays $15 an hour for 20 hours a week (an example). The worker earns 15 times 20, or $300 a week before taxes.

Wages follow supply and demand. When many people can do a job and few businesses need it, wages tend to be lower. When a job needs rare skills, like a nurse or electrician, and many employers need them, wages tend to be higher. Training and education often raise what a worker can earn.

A *labor union* is a group of workers who join together to bargain with an employer about wages, hours and safety. Bargaining as a group is called collective bargaining. Supporters say unions give workers a stronger voice and better pay. Critics say they can raise costs, which may lead firms to hire fewer workers. Economists study and debate both effects, including the effects of the federal minimum wage, which has been $7.25 an hour since 2009.

words.d: the payment a worker earns for work, often counted per hour
a group of workers who join together to bargain with employers about pay, hours and working conditions
talks between a union and an employer to agree on wages and working conditions

look.title: Two Job Offers
look.text: Carlos gets two summer job offers (example wages). A grocery store pays $14 an hour for 25 hours a week. A lifeguard job pays $17 an hour for 20 hours, but he must first take a certification class.
look.prompt: Which job pays more per week? Why might the lifeguard job pay a higher hourly wage?

check.q: A worker earns $16 an hour and works 25 hours (example wage). What does she earn before taxes?
check.why: 16 times 25 equals $400.

check.q: Why do jobs that need rare skills usually pay higher wages?
choices: Few workers can do them, and many employers need them
check.why: A small supply of skilled workers and a high demand for them push wages up.

check.q: What is one argument critics make about unions?
choices: Higher costs may lead firms to hire fewer workers
Unions are the same as monopolies on goods
check.why: Critics argue that union-won wage gains raise costs, which can reduce hiring. Supporters stress better pay and voice.

review.q: A school store takes in $500 and has $380 in costs (example amounts). What is its profit?
review.why: Profit equals revenue minus costs: $500 minus $380 equals $120.

review.q: Which business type gives owners limited liability?
choices: A lemonade stand run by one person
review.why: Corporation shareholders can lose only what they invested.

review.q: A shop sells 80 caps at $12 each (example price). What is its revenue?
review.why: Revenue is price times quantity: 80 times $12 equals $960.

review.q: Only one company sells electricity in a region, and there is no close substitute. What is this market?
review.why: A single seller with no close substitutes is a monopoly.

review.q: A second school store opens and cuts the price of water. What does this show?
review.why: A rival seller competing for buyers pushes prices down.

review.q: Which is a fixed cost for the school store?
choices: The monthly rent for the room
The chips it buys to resell
review.why: Rent stays the same no matter how much the store sells.

review.q: What is the main purpose of antitrust laws?
choices: To protect competition and stop price-fixing
review.why: Antitrust laws ban actions like price-fixing that block competition and hurt buyers.

review.q: An entrepreneur spends $500 on supplies and earns $350 in sales (example amounts). What is the result?
review.why: Costs are bigger than revenue: $500 minus $350 equals a loss of $150.
